title_en: Who Is the Real Liberation Army?
excerpt_en: A year after Maduro's capture, the U.S.-published escrow ledger shows $12.26 billion in Venezuelan oil money — 98.6% of it disbursed back to Venezuela. Growth hit 7.42%, wages are rising, and 82% of Venezuelans back the oil deal. So who liberated whom?
body_en:
A year ago, when news broke that Maduro had been captured, plenty of Western analysts predicted chaos for Venezuela — civil war, even. A year on, reality has flipped the script. The country did not descend into chaos. Life there has visibly improved — and not on anyone's aid money, but on its own oil revenue, with every dollar accounted for in a public ledger.

Where the oil money went: $12.26 billion, 98.6% of it back to Venezuela

Start with the hard numbers. The U.S. State Department recently published the full report on Venezuela's escrow account, laying out the books for February through September of this year: a total of $12.26372 billion flowed into the account, all of it from compliant Venezuelan oil and mining transactions. Of that, $12.111 billion has already been disbursed to Venezuela's interim government. By the end of September, only about $160 million remained in the account, waiting to be claimed.

In other words, 98.6% of the money earned from selling oil ended up in Venezuelan hands. The escrow account is a bookkeeping mechanism, watched end to end by the U.S. State and Treasury Departments for compliance. The online claim that "America pocketed all of Venezuela's oil money" does not survive contact with this ledger.

What price the oil fetched: heavy crude at no discount, riding a war premium

The money was not pocketed — but did it fetch a fair price? According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, Venezuela exported roughly 123.9 million barrels of crude in the first nine months of this year, more than double its entire previous year. Since most of the escrow funds are crude revenue, that works out to about $99 a barrel.

Venezuela produces heavy sour crude, which historically trades $8 to $12 below Brent. But this year, with Middle Eastern heavy crude supply cut off and refiners worldwide scrambling for feedstock, Venezuelan oil stopped selling at a discount — at times it even priced above benchmark, soaking up the war premium in full. In the week ending October 2, Venezuela shipped 624,000 barrels a day to the United States, holding its seat as America's second-largest oil supplier for over half a year. Average daily exports this year reached 458,000 barrels, up 227% from the same period in 2023.

How life is going: 7.42% growth, wage hikes scheduled into next year

The economic data is even more direct. Latin American institutions had forecast 6.5% growth for Venezuela this year; central bank figures put third-quarter growth at 7.42%, first in Latin America — achieved, no less, under the strain of post-earthquake reconstruction. Oil production has climbed from 700,000 barrels a day to 1.236 million in September, with a year-end target of 1.4 million. International oil firms have signed cooperation deals, and refining capacity is set to double next year.

Living standards are being repaired too. On April 30, the government raised the combined minimum income from $190 to $240, up 26.3%, and the minimum pension to $70. Fuller wallets revived consumption: national supermarket sales are now a full half higher than under Maduro. On October 30, acting president Rodríguez announced four wage increases for workers in 2027, indexed to economic growth — nothing like the old model of printing money and watching inflation dissolve every raise. This time the route is steady growth.

Public opinion: 82% back the oil deal, 91% back dialogue with the U.S.

Rodríguez called the energy cooperation agreement "historic": within a few short months, restrained negotiation turned a grim standoff into room for mutually beneficial cooperation, and the two sides also agreed to restart military-technical cooperation. Washington, for its part, hopes the arrangement reduces the Strait of Hormuz's leverage over the Americas.

The polling says even more. In September, the Hinterlaces polling firm ran a nationwide survey: 82% of Venezuelans support the oil agreement with the United States, 91% view dialogue with Washington favorably, and most people do not want to go back. Eight months of oil exports to the U.S. earned $12.3 billion, growth leads Latin America, and wage hikes are scheduled across all four quarters of next year. People are voting with their feet, and the vote is clear.

So who is the real liberation army?

"Liberation" is a word that has been shouted for decades. By the old script, when Americans seize a country's president and reach into its oil accounts, that is textbook imperialist plunder, and resistance and civil war should follow. The script did not play out that way: the money — 98.6% of it — went back; the oil sold for more than it used to; wages, for the first time, are being negotiated ahead of inflation; and the ledger, for the first time, is fully public for anyone to audit.

Where did the prophets of civil war go wrong? They assumed sanctions and external blockade were what crushed this country. What actually crushed it was a regime that turned oil wealth into a private ATM and the printing press into a finance ministry. Once that regime fell, even an interim government propped up by the "invader" could change daily life overnight — as long as the oil money actually returned to ordinary people.

So the question stands: who is the real liberation army? The man who shouted anti-imperialist slogans while supermarket shelves stood empty, or the "invader" who wired $12.2 billion back, transfer by transfer, into the country's account? Liberation was never about whose slogans are loudest or whose flag flies highest. It is about whose arrival makes ordinary people's bowls fuller. Whoever lets the people live better is the liberator — regardless of nationality, regardless of flag.

And turn it around: a regime that can only hold on by blocking information and scaring people with "the Americans are coming to steal the oil" was never afraid of invaders. It is afraid that once its people taste a better life, they will realize they never needed it at all.
